#Specialized_Viewpoint 808 #Elite_Diplomacy #International

🔰 National Media: Success by the Yardstick of Information Dissemination or Narrative-Building?

👤 Seyed Amir Yahyavi, a researcher at the Sharif Governance Think Tank, has written a note in Farhikhtegan as part of a special feature titled "Politics in the Mirror":

🔹 The two domains of "news reporting" and "analysis/narrative-building" are distinct from one another. Although IRIB's access to official sources and first-hand information is a significant advantage and has at times led to international re-publication, it alone is not a sign of success in the narrative battlefield.

🔸 Major international media have turned themselves into arenas where different narratives confront one another; meanwhile, the prevailing model in the national media remains inviting like-minded experts and confronting the rival narrative through mockery or dismissal. Critiquing the rival narrative is essential; but without understanding, distinguishing, and constructing an alternative narrative, persuading an unsympathetic audience will be difficult.

🔹 Success in the war of narratives requires producing an authentic narrative, creating a space for genuine confrontation of viewpoints, and moving beyond reactive caution to active narrative engagement.

🗞️Published in: Farhikhtegan

🔰Economic Literacy: A Mission for the National Media

👤Amirhossein Gholipour, a researcher in the Economy Group, has contributed a note to Farhikhtegan as part of a special feature titled "Politics in the Mirror":

🔹Beyond news, entertainment, and coverage of daily controversies, the national media can see itself as an institution that grows society's stock of knowledge—a stock that cannot be summoned overnight when an economic crisis hits, energy prices are reformed, a currency decision is made, or the pension system is overhauled.

🔸Perhaps the measure of success for such an approach is precisely this: not that the audience necessarily ends up agreeing with the government once the program is over, but that they can say, "Now I have a better grasp of what the problem is, who bears the costs, who stands to gain, and what consequences the options before the country would have." If the national media can make that sentence part of the everyday experience of millions of Iranians, then raising awareness will no longer be a mere byproduct of the media; it will become one of its most vital public services and one of the foundations of reform and better governance.
